title: When the Front Line Gives Way — A Roman Relief Manoeuvre
primary_sources: Polybius, Histories, Book VI (The Roman Military System)
Titus Livius (Livy), Ab Urbe Condita, Book VIII, Chapter 8 (The Manipular Battle Order)
scholarly_references: Adrian Goldsworthy, The Complete Roman Army (2003)
Philip Sabin, The Mechanics of Battle in Antiquity (2000)
reconstruction_disclaimer: This video depicts an illustrative reconstruction of a tactical line-relief manoeuvre based on Polybius and Livy, not a minute-by-minute attested recording of a specific historical battle.

claims.claim: An opening in the Roman line looks like the end. But watch what happens behind the shields.
Across the field, enemy warbands charge forward in a violent surge.
The front rank Hastati brace, locking their scuta against the incoming assault.
The two battle lines collide with brutal force, shields shuddering under the impact.
Under continuous pressure, the frontline soldiers struggle and begin to fatigue.
Behind them, the centurion sounds a sharp horn blast, ordering an immediate relief.
A narrow corridor opens between the front files, parting the Roman shield wall.
The exhausted defenders slip backward through the gap along a clear withdrawal path.
Fresh Princeps from the second line march forward, advancing into the vacated positions.
The reserves close shields into an unbreakable wall, repelling the enemy counter-thrust.
An overhead tactical view reveals how the Roman manipular system preserved fighting stamina.
